heading: Streaming
body:
StreamRoute marks a controller method that answers GET requests with a stream. The method yields values from a private generator that holds the loop. Each value becomes one limited server-sent event, a message that the server pushes over an open HTTP response. When the method finishes, the server sends an end event, so the browser does not reconnect. The method name starts with stream. A generator under GetRoute is refused, so one marker says that a route streams. JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Kotlin, C#, F#, Dart, Ruby, Lua and Go support this. Lua sends each value with `coroutine.yield`, because Tachyon runs the route in a coroutine. A Go stream method returns `iter.Seq[Tick]`, Go's own generator: its function calls `yield` once for each value and stops when `yield` returns false. Return `iter.Seq2[Tick, error]` when the stream can fail; an error ends the stream with an error event. Java, Groovy and Rust have no generator, so they refuse StreamRoute with TY2015 and return once. A stream has the same time limit as every request. At the limit, Tachyon stops the process and sends an error event, and the browser opens the stream again. When the reader goes away, Tachyon stops the process at once. A Go method that takes the `*http.Request` can read the time limit from `request.Context()`. The context ends just before the limit, so a stream that should finish there, such as a log follow, returns and sends the end event instead.

C++ has no tab here, because C++ Yon code has only route controllers so far: the build refuses `StreamRoute` in C++ with `TY2015` (ADR 0099).
